# Claim adjudication table

Every claim below was checked against the cited evidence. `Partially supported`
means a kernel of truth exists but the claim as commonly stated overstates it.
`False` is reserved for claims the evidence contradicts, not merely claims that
are unproven.

| # | Claim | Category | Verdict | What the evidence shows | Sources |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Magnesium glycinate is the most absorbable form. | Formulation | **Unsupported** | There is no reliable head-to-head evidence in healthy adults showing glycinate beats citrate or other soluble salts. In the one trial that compared glycinate with oxide, absorption was identical overall and better only in patients with severe malabsorption. | R07, R09 |
| 2 | Magnesium oxide is useless because it is poorly absorbed. | Formulation | **Partially supported** | Oxide is the least bioavailable common form, at roughly 4% absorption versus 9-11% for soluble salts, and it often fails to raise serum magnesium. It still delivers magnesium and is the standard form in several positive trials and in constipation products, so 'useless' overstates a real disadvantage. | R03, R05, R15 |
| 3 | Magnesium citrate is one of the better-absorbed forms. | Formulation | **Supported** | Citrate consistently beats oxide on urinary recovery and serum magnesium, and it is soluble across gastric pH. The size of the advantage is modest, roughly 14 mg more urinary magnesium per day in one trial. | R04, R05, R06 |
| 4 | Chelated magnesium is absorbed better than non-chelated magnesium. | Formulation | **Partially supported** | 'Chelate' is a chemical description, not a guarantee. Albion-style glycinate chelates are well tolerated and absorb well, but trials do not show a consistent advantage over citrate, and some products labelled chelate contain mostly oxide. | R07, R46 |
| 5 | Magnesium prevents or treats muscle cramps. | Performance | **Unsupported** | In idiopathic cramps, mainly in older adults, magnesium reduced cramps by about 0.18 per week, a difference that is not statistically or clinically meaningful. Pregnancy data are inconsistent, and the largest nocturnal-cramp trial was stopped for futility. | R11, R12, R14 |
| 6 | Magnesium relieves leg cramps in pregnancy. | Performance | **Partially supported** | Trials disagree: some show fewer cramps and others show none, and meta-analysis finds no significant reduction. A clinician may still trial it because it is low risk, but the evidence is weak. | R12, R13 |
| 7 | Magnesium cures insomnia. | Performance | **Partially supported** | Small trials in older adults and poor sleepers show modest improvements, including about 17 minutes faster sleep onset in a pooled analysis of three small trials, but certainty is low to very low and several trials in other populations are null. It is not a treatment for insomnia disorder. | R15, R16, R17, R18 |
| 8 | Magnesium bisglycinate is proven to improve sleep. | Performance | **Partially supported** | A 2025 placebo-controlled trial found a statistically significant but small effect on insomnia severity (about 1.6 points, d=0.2). One trial is not proof, and the effect is smaller than the placebo response. | R17 |
| 9 | Magnesium is an effective treatment for anxiety. | Performance | **Partially supported** | Trials suggest small benefits, especially in people with low magnesium status or high stress, but samples are small, formulas vary, and several trials are null. It is not a substitute for evidence-based anxiety treatment. | R25, R26, R27 |
| 10 | Magnesium treats depression. | Performance | **Partially supported** | Pooled trials show moderate symptom reductions, but heterogeneity is high and most studies are small or adjunctive. It may help as an add-on in deficiency, not as a stand-alone antidepressant. | R28 |
| 11 | Magnesium prevents migraines. | Performance | **Partially supported** | At 600 mg/day of trimagnesium dicitrate, one good trial cut attack frequency by 41.6% versus 15.8% with placebo, and guidelines give it a Level B or Grade C recommendation. Effect sizes are modest, formulation matters, and the dose exceeds the supplemental upper limit. | R19, R20, R21 |
| 12 | Magnesium lowers blood pressure. | Performance | **Partially supported** | Pooled trials show reductions of about 2 mmHg systolic and 1.8-2 mmHg diastolic overall, with larger effects (up to about 7.7 mmHg systolic) in treated hypertensives and people with low magnesium. Normotensive people see little or no change. | R22, R23, R24 |
| 13 | Magnesium supplements prevent heart attacks and strokes. | Performance | **Unsupported** | Cohort studies link higher magnesium intake and serum levels to lower cardiovascular risk, but no adequately powered randomised trial shows that supplements prevent events. Guideline claims are about adequate dietary intake, not supplementation. | R01, R22 |
| 14 | Magnesium L-threonate boosts memory and brain function. | Performance | **Unsupported** | The human literature is a handful of small, mostly industry-funded trials with inconsistent results and no measurement of brain magnesium. The largest recent trial found a borderline effect on one composite and null results on most secondary outcomes. | R33, R34, R35, R36 |
| 15 | Magnesium L-threonate crosses the blood-brain barrier better than other forms. | Formulation | **Partially supported** | Animal studies show higher brain magnesium with threonate, which is a plausible mechanism. Human brain magnesium has not been measured, so the marketing claim is an extrapolation. | R34, R37 |
| 16 | A 2 g dose of magnesium L-threonate is a high magnesium dose. | Formulation | **False** | Two grams of Magtein contains only about 144 mg of elemental magnesium, because the commercial salt is roughly 7% magnesium by weight. That is under half the daily RDA and less than many 400 mg oxide tablets. | R37 |
| 17 | Sixty to seventy-five per cent of people are magnesium deficient. | Safety | **False** | About 48% of Americans consume less than the Estimated Average Requirement from food, which is not the same as clinical deficiency. Symptomatic deficiency is uncommon in healthy people because the kidneys conserve magnesium. | R01, R56 |
| 18 | A blood magnesium test tells you whether you need magnesium. | Safety | **False** | Serum holds less than 1% of body magnesium and is tightly regulated, so a normal level can coexist with tissue depletion. No single test is satisfactory; assessment needs diet, risk factors and sometimes red-cell or loading tests. | R01, R51 |
| 19 | You need 400 mg of magnesium from a supplement every day. | Safety | **False** | The 310-420 mg RDA covers all sources, including food. The supplemental upper limit for adults is 350 mg/day, so a 400 mg supplement exceeds it unless a clinician directs otherwise. | R01, R02 |
| 20 | Magnesium is natural, so it is safe at any dose. | Safety | **False** | High doses cause diarrhoea and, in kidney impairment, dangerous hypermagnesemia with hypotension, respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Cases have been fatal, including at 3000 mg/day of hydroxide. | R01, R44, R45 |
| 21 | Magnesium supplements damage healthy kidneys. | Safety | **False** | Healthy kidneys excrete excess magnesium efficiently. The risk runs the other way: impaired kidney function causes accumulation, so magnesium should be supervised or avoided in CKD depending on eGFR. | R01, R42, R43 |
| 22 | Magnesium glycinate never causes digestive upset. | Safety | **Partially supported** | Glycinate is generally better tolerated than oxide or citrate, but any osmotically active magnesium dose can loosen stools, and large glycinate doses still cause diarrhoea in some people. | R07, R01 |
| 23 | Topical magnesium oil or Epsom salt baths raise magnesium levels. | Formulation | **Unsupported** | Intact skin is nearly impermeable to magnesium; ex vivo work finds negligible permeation, and a placebo-controlled cream trial found no significant overall rise in serum magnesium. Any perceived benefit is unlikely to be magnesium replacement. | R38, R39, R40 |
| 24 | Epsom salt baths relieve cramps by replacing magnesium. | Formulation | **Unsupported** | There is no controlled evidence that bathing raises magnesium status enough to matter. Warm water and relaxation may help symptoms independently of magnesium. | R38, R40 |
| 25 | Magnesium must be taken with calcium in a fixed ratio. | Formulation | **Unsupported** | The body regulates calcium and magnesium separately. There is no established requirement for a 1:1 or 2:1 ratio in supplements, and high-dose calcium can compete with magnesium absorption. | R01, R08 |
| 26 | Vitamin B6 is needed for magnesium absorption. | Formulation | **Partially supported** | B6 does not increase intestinal magnesium absorption. In stressed adults with low magnesium, adding B6 improved some symptom scores more than magnesium alone, which is a separate effect, not an absorption requirement. | R26 |
| 27 | High-dose zinc does not affect magnesium. | Safety | **Unsupported** | A zinc intake of 142 mg/day disrupted magnesium balance in a controlled study. People taking high-dose zinc for other reasons should not assume magnesium status is unaffected. | R01 |
| 28 | A third-party seal proves the supplement works. | Cost | **False** | Certification verifies identity, strength and contaminant limits, not clinical benefit. A certified product with a poor dose or an inferior form is still a poor choice. | R47, R46 |
| 29 | More expensive magnesium is better magnesium. | Cost | **False** | Price per elemental milligram varies 37-fold in this sample, and the cheapest products were oxide and malate, not the premium chelates. Cost tracks marketing and format more than evidence. | R46 |
| 30 | A magnesium complex with several forms is better than one form. | Formulation | **Unsupported** | Blends can be reasonable, but they often hide low elemental doses behind long ingredient lists and make it impossible to know what was tested. There is no evidence that combining salts improves outcomes. | R09, R48 |
| 31 | A higher-milligram magnesium supplement is stronger. | Formulation | **False** | What matters is elemental magnesium absorbed, and fractional absorption falls as the dose rises. A 400 mg oxide tablet may deliver less usable magnesium than a divided 200 mg citrate dose, while causing more diarrhoea. | R03, R08 |
